As for the goods pitched on, I only desire what you think convenient, part, all, or more, as you please. I've got a boat, which I'll send when you please.
I've had a letter from Sherlock that they cant come till Monday, but then will fall on, pell mell. I've sent for the windows etc.
I think to get the hall floor laid and that particon taken down immediately. The hall floor cant be settled unless all windows altered, so pray your full orders per next.
We viewed Tumby since we came home. I like it better and better every time I see it.

Our humble duty attend your self and dear mother and sister. I hope we shall get all things in tolerable order against Midsummer, the time you apoint for your coming down. I am, dear Sir, your most dutiful son and obedient humble servant, J. Banks.
I've got you an horse which I believe will fit you very well. Otherways when you see him we can sell him again.

note.value: 51. JOHN SHERLOCK TO JOSEPH BANKS I.

text.p: Revesby, 30 April 1717. Yesterday Mr. Banks wrote about the best chamber, and hope shall have your answer. The chimney in the dining room won't be in the middle.

With advice of Mr. Banks and lady (if you please to admit on it) to make a drawing room over the cellar, this chimney will fit it and there is a convenient place on the wing of the chimney to make one for the dining room.
And when you please to build another wing to answer the last it may be a bedchamber below and dressing room and closett above. This will be a very good house without any further adishon.

If we've good success in taking down this wall (which I don't fear) we've another project which I think you'll like, that is to take down the other wall in the hall and build a place without the house to remove the stairs whole into, which will make the hall a large room. And I'm, with all duty, your honor's humble servant, Jno Sherlock.

note.value: 54. JOSEPH BANKS II TO JOSEPH BANKS I.

text.p: Revesby, 15 May 1717 . I humbly thank for your kind offer of one of the best beds (we should have been very well content with the old bed as in last), so my wife pitches of the kalomanco bed, but shall want some little stuff thats near of the colour to hang out the room, the quantity of which I'll send to you as soon as I have measured it. We shall want one feather bed and the chairs you mention, but pray have regard to the paper of things we pitched on about 5 or 6 posts agon, being mostly such things as would be useful to us and sell but for little. Pray remember cabinets and chest of drawers for your own use.

I likewise thank you for the marble harth, and desire you'd buy me one stove grate with one fender and set of utensils as poker tongs fireshovell and belows, and pack them in the half hogsheads, and if you please the spices in another, that I send a catalogue of in my next.
I never had my deeds for the Door estate from you. They are, I believe, in your iron chest at Scofton. Pray push R. Clay on, if he can sell it for its worth.
Pray leave no stone unturnd in this affair of Howbrigs. We'll spare for no charges to do our selves justice, which I'm sensible has not been done us hitherto.

The lime and bricks are going about with all expedition. I cannot hear of my friend (since my return) who manages Coap's farm. He's taken a ramble to see some relation, but I'll watch his return. I have got the £50 from Soresby. Many thanks to you are due.
I sent of Monday for the Tax Act but could not hear of it, have sent an especial messenger to day, and Mr. Short is by appointment to be with me to day to read it together.

Yesterday I went to Mr. Wright, who said he was sending you a pretty good return just then. Since you design to be down so soon, I think will respitt that affair, for it must run in another channel, unavoidably.
Eager of Moreby gave Mr. Wright no notice of leaving his farm till the day before Martinmas day, so that we're of opinion we can force him to hold it another year.

I'm in no want of either hay or corn, and you may depend upon it all things shall be provided for your reception. I'll get the barn done and trust to your generosity. I'll take care of lime and of Cope too.

Our attorney for How Briggs never could get a copy of the indictment tho he demanded it twice, which we take to be another reason why they should not give judgment against us; so without further order I will not ask for a copy of the indictment, fearing it may prejudice us.

Mr. Sherlock and I have just been talking over the model in yours of the 5th, and since we've not time to do anything but finish our present undertaking, so we can take more time to consider of it, only desire your positive answer whether the chimney shall be removed or stand as it does, and have 2 wainscott pillors put up as in your last. The enclosed is the wages which I think more than Mr. Sherlock talked of or writ, one of the 2, but I can't find the letter. I've spoke to him. He says they never have less. I can't say but they are diligent understanding men and work from 5 to 7. Pray your thoughts of it, and send me back the bill.
Our humble duty attend you, dear Mother, and sister. My mother I'll send her affectionate service as due. I am, your most dutiful son and obedient servant, J. Banks.
Pray what becomes of Cuss: Hancock? I wish you could do something for him.

note.value: 55. JOSEPH BANKS II TO JOSEPH BANKS I.

text.p:
Revesby, 19 May 1717. Upon peruseing the Land Tax, we found it quite altered to what it was before, and if you look page 214
you'll find their is time given till the 29 September, so that we shall have time enough to consider of this after you come down and my neighbour Short retourns home, and the Act is so very exact that we shall have occasion to lay all our heads together.

As to Parson Cope I've been with him, and he seems very civil, told me he had not his writings in his own hands, but would send for the lease and show it me in a little time. I discharged the milner from workeing up the wood, but it went against my conscience, for I never saw a milne so much out of repair. In short twil cost as much to repair as to build it from the ground.

I desire to have a pair of fine wasted hoes the same of the cloth. Pray order your servant to write 2 lines to Waddell himself. I delivered the silver hilt to the wagoner himself, gave him sixpence and he promised to deliver it to you himself.

The 10 inches of wall shall be put up again, 'twil be as soon done as spoke of. It was part taken down before your letter came. I'm very sorry you should seem so very angry at so small a transgression. I'll assure you your orders shall be observed as nearly as may be for the future, for I am far from contradicting your orders in these affairs, that was it not for your goodness and generosity I should never alter anything.

I design to take a butler that is a gardiner, so if you please should be very thankful if your engage me Tom, Mr. Jaqueline's nephew, who is now gardiner att Scofton, I shall be obliged to you. If you please send him the enclosed letter and add what you seem convenient to it, I've forgot his surname.

Your tenant Clarke grows so very infirm with the continual pains of the stone that he desires to resign his farm, and young Tom James will hold it if you think fit. They have both been with me. I believe he'll be a very good tenant.

We rejoice to hear my mother is so much better, pray God continue it. Our most affectionate duty, love and service attend you, dear Mother and sister, as due, I am, honoured Sir, your most dutiful son and affectionate servant, J. Banks.
Enclosed is the list of the groceries etc. which we desire you'll please to buy for us, and send in an half hogshead.

note.value: 56. JOHN SHERLOCK TO JOSEPH BANKS I.

text.p:
According to your order I've sent the bearer and by him a small token of oysters which I desire you'll accept. I've thought what you said in making the new wing an apartment which will be very good and may bring the bed chamber to the stair head and have the dressing room and dark closett at the other end. I had forgot to speak about the old windows, I could a disposed of 'em in summer and may be I can the next, but desire to know the price. I think you'll have occasion for most on 'em your self. You said it was your desire to have the old account set stright.
Please to leave order by your son, and if you find anything in it that is not fair make what abatement you please. It may be you'll think my assistance too much, but I've not set down half my journeys. The sashes I got nothing by and Mr. Banks can tell you what I got by my men. However I'm willing to serve you as I have done. Sir, her's two bills, one as my book is, the other cost a guiney. Your direction about it shall be observed and acknowledged a great favour done to your honor's humble servant, Jno Sherlock.

note.value: 57. JOSEPH BANKS II TO JOSEPH BANKS I.

text.p: 5 June 1717 . If the proposal for dear sisters M-h be pleasing to you and agreeable to her, we shall be extremely glad and most heartily wish success to it.
Enclosed is the copy of our indictment. I could not possibly get it before.
I am surprised att what Marshall wrote to you. He told me the ladies were his relations. Isle write to him again myself, and will endeavour to find out who Cope pays rent to.
We kept no copy of the note for groceries but will guess att it, viz consider as we did before what we want .

I was yesterday with Mr. Wright who is trifles, but yet I do not think fit to quarrel right with him. Iv spoke to Kirkham to pay you £60 next Friday seven-night which he says he'll do if his man has not .... of retourns in his way to London, and Mr. Wright has promised me the monies and says he will send you all he has, but he's nothing but shuffle, and theirs no dependence on his word, but since you are to be down so shortly, I would not have any bustle made, for then you may take your accounts and your affairs out of his hands.

Michael will manage the receiving of the rents very well, but I can't spare him any further att all, for he manages all business att home and never stirs out except to wait of his mistress when she dines with a neighbour or so; so that I doubt you can have little use of him in any other capacity, for now hay time and harvest is coming on that he'll be continually engaged but att meal times.

was here yesterday and has turned his to me, so that now their wages are pretty reasonable, so that I shall not change them. They now have one shilling, 3d. a peace less then before. We have finished the best chamber and all that alteration except laying the floor and a little matter of the wainscott in the new dining room, so that I hope we shall have things in tolerable readiness by Midsummer or a week after.

The boat man that was to've brought my goods from Scofton has sent me word their is not passing Fossdyke, and Iv sent thither and find it too true, so that I must fetch my goods by land carriage, which I think I can do pretty reasonably, only I cant bring the malt, so desire it may be either kept for me till a boat will come, or else sell it their. But pray in your next be pleased to tell me what goods I may bring from Scofton for I think either to go or send Michael to see them packed up, and I think to get them brought by that carries wool to Wakefield, weeks time.

I've put my coach cart mares in pretty good order. I never have them very poor. You talk as if corn was cheap with you, tic far otherwise here, oats are the lowest 12s. per quarter and wheat £2 3s. 0d. per quarter. I am glad youve sold your stock to the Brigadier for our fen is but very indiferent, and I'm afraid their'l be great loss. One of your mares was very near dying but, we've recovered her, but I've one fallen ill myself that I doubt will dye.
The brick goas forward apace, and I hope will prove very good.
Our most affectionate duty love and service attend yourself, dear momma, and sister. I am, dear Sir, your most dutiful son and servant, J. Banks.

note.value: 58. JOSEPH BANKS II TO JOSEPH BANKS I.

text.p: Revesby, 29 June 1717. Enclosed is an exact account of what I've brought from Scofton, which I hope will be agreeable to your commands. I fancy when the cabinets drawers etc. are brought twill be the safest and best way to bring them all along by land carriage. The best great bell I've brought away, and you may certainly take away the other, for they are no ways fastened to the freehold. I've likewise ordered the bowls to be set by for your use, tho the Brigadier said he was to have them, but I do not find that by the articles. We've cleared Mother closett as you ordered for Mrs. Sutton, and return you a 1000 thanks for all these great favours.

My neighbour Campsall came to speak to me about driveing the sheep. I doubt he's a villain, and the rest not much better by his talk, for he says Will kept a cow or 2 all winter of your hay, and that he can tell of other misdemeanours. When knaves fall out honest folk will come to their right.
Mr. Stevens met me here last night just as I came home and is going about his business.
I'll take care of the writ of error as you direct.
I know not what to say about Joseph. I doubt he's but a drunken carlos fellow, and for his abilities in looking after horses I know nothing, tho he's very tractable and willing.
Our most humble duty and affectionate service attends you dear mother and sister, and I am, dear Sir, your most dutiful son and obliged servant, J. Banks.
I've bought no yett ewes, for had bought in my full quantity before I received your letter.
You've one score of sheep very fat, which I advised Mr. Langley to sell, and the rest will be fat in 6 weeks time.

note.value: 61. THE REV. JOSEPH COPE TO JOSEPH BANKS I.

text.p:
Kirkby on Been, 4 July 1717. I would gladly have waited upon you at Reavesby, but I am not able to go or ride so far by reason of my great weakness and many infirmities and old age. Sir, I understand that there is great need of more timber to finish the repairs of Tumby mills; and if you please out of your own generosity will order some timber to complete the work, no man shall be more thankful to you for it then myself. By the late owners that I farmed it of I was to have all timber found me, but what your covenants are about it I neither doe desire to know nor to make any question of it, but you will doe what is just. I should be very desirous to see you at Kirkby; if not I
would endeavour to waite of you at Tumby if I can possibly get so far, who am your most humble servant and tenant whilst, Jose: Cope.

note.value: 62. JOSEPH BANKS II TO JOSEPH BANKS I.

text.p: 6 July 1717. I see by yours of the 27 June which is the last I received that you thought I had marked too many things as you well might, But I dare say you scarce thought so when you saw the inventory of what I brought away. The reason of my markeing so many things in the inventory was, that I thought by some of your former letters you seemed to think you would live att Revesby the most of the time you will be in the country, except some little time att Hurne which place I fancied you'd have had furnished in such manner as to have been in a tolerable condition to have received you, but as I hope that I've taken nothing away att present but what you will like of, so will pursue your further directions for what you would have done.

Pray what do you do about Lord Harborough's estate? It will vex you if it be bought out of our hands. I can't yett find out who Cope pays his rent too for the Ladies farm in Revesby, the enclosed I received from him of Thursday which you must pray give an answer too by the return of the post. I scarce know how to advise you for the milne takes as much repairing as if it was to be built new, the goits, dams, soles and wheels and everything being made new. I go now and then to see they do what they do do, substantially, but if you can force him to repair with his own wood, I would have you doubtless to do it, otherways you better let him have a little wood then let the milne be unfinished.

My wife joins with me in humble duty to yourself, dear mother, and affectionate love to dear sister. Pray how goes on her match? We should be glad to hear, heartily wishing it may be to all our satisfactions. I am, dear Sir, your most dutiful son and obedient humble servant, J. Banks.

My wife will write to my mother next post. Your monies comes in but slowly, but however I've laid wait for returns and will pay them the monies as I get it. You must order that affair positively when you come down.

note.value: 66. JOHN SHERLOCK TO JOSEPH BANKS I.

text.p:
20 Jan. 1718? I had yours this day seven night that you left for me when you went from Reavsby. I'm sorry you should complain of my bill. Mr. Banks knows what I got by my men. He did say there wages was thought to be unreasonable, so I desired him to get other hands as soon as he could. I would not have the work stopped and told him he might pay these as I did (till then), but he got none and I lost there summer for I wanted 'em at home where our wages is paid without abatement. The removing the stairs you was not charged with. The modilion cornice you agreed it should be put about the end, but it was such an od thing we did not know what to do. All was done by your consent and if you think fit to make abatement for this and the alteration of the summer tree do as you please: as to the wast about the colour know nothing on it only a little Wm Green brought
that was valued at 18d.: as to the work coming to more by day then square I can't help. You may please to remember I often wrote and told you such alterations and jobs could not be taken. I know I gave rates of new work and you set 'em down and the sash windows at 30s. a piece, but you sent me London rates and I charged you the same. I acknowledge a mistake in my bills for the 13 of May. I did not set down my men's time for that week, and when that and for my time is added I believe they'll be right. I did not set down half the times I was there, and if you don't think I deserve so much give me what you please. I beg our accounts may be set stright. The next sashes will pay for the old transoms. I desire to know the price. I can justly say if you pay the whole bill I don't get one farding by it neither do I desire it for what is past nor for what is to come, for it may be in your power to do me kindnesses and in particular something I have in hand about the breach at Dagenham. I think you know it has runt several years and has been offen attempted and all has miscarried as well as Capt Perry the last year (experance has taught me I can stop it). I've wrote to him that I will give him proposals to his satisfaction. I believe he will give me answer. I don't do it to lessen him in any respect. I shall make bold to let you how the matter goes, and am with duty your honor's most humble servant, Jno Sherlock.

note.value: 67. JOSEPH BANKS II TO JOSEPH BANKS I.

text.p: Revesby, 24 January 1718. I enquired of Mr. Wright what became of the windfalls. He says their was but one ash worth anything, and we had it sawne into joists for Sandam's house. I'll sell but few ashes this year, but will try both ways, viz whether it be better to sell them standing or worked up, so by that means I shall know better against another year. I would gladly have your advice before we sell many, for it will disfigure the grounds mightily.

By the enclosed note you'll see what I've done with Parson Whelpdale, so I shall take care to let his farm to advantage for the ensuing year, and you must set your reckoning straight when you come down into these parts. He seems very civil, and says he'll submit all to you when you come down.

I've appointed your tenants to pay me their rents of Tuesday and Wedensday next, tho I am afraid they will not all pay. However, I've ordered Mr. Stevens to pay you on my account 15£ and I've ordered 50 or 60£ more to come to you speedily out of Derbyshire, and I've laid wait for retourns here, which are exceeding scarce. However, I'll always take care to send you monies as soon as it comes to my hands, and will make up and send you your accounts as soon as this half year is pretty nigh got in, and anything more you please to command me.

Here is about 40 or 50£ per annum upon sale in East Kirkby, but the title is upon the same hold with Parson West's estate there. They ask 20 years purchase. I fancy I could buy it for 19. It's some little to be improved, but not much, but for the title you are the best judge. You must give me speedy orders about it, for I've but time till I hear from you before they will publicly offer it to the best bidder, tho perhaps chapman will not be plenty full on account of the title.
Poor Widow Lamin wants to take administration to her husband's effects. Pray have not you a power as successor to the Abott to grant administrations, or must she apply to Doctors' Commons?

I beg you'd be so kind as to buy me livery cloth lineing and buttons for 2 men's liveries and let it be sent down by the carrier. If there be half a yard to spare I should have use for it, hat lace and buttons for 2 hats if you please.
Pray tell Mr. Chapman I'm ashamed sent his monies. My illness has prevented me, but the first bill I can get I'll return it him. Pray my kind service to him.

Pray what hopes of the loins? Is not Lord S-d married? What says Lord Molesworth? Sure faith has left the earth, and in time we shall all be dogs chopping in the baskett for our own bellies. I am, dear Sir, your most dutiful son and obedient humble servant, J. Banks.

Tom Henley is run his country having got 7 or 8 in people's debt both here and at Maram. He went the day before Xmas but we expected his return till last week, so I must be forced to set some one else on. He only finished the staircase and best parlour shutters.

note.value: 68. JOSEPH BANKS I TO JOHN SHERLOCK.

text.p:
28 January 1718. I am surprised at what you write of my letter coming so late to you. Surely it was occasioned by my son's illness, to whom I have wrote this post, to make an end of
it with you, for its now all out of my hands, not having your bills nor my own remarks, but this I can remember, the wainscott and every thing else came to double the usual prices allowing for jobs and alterations, so you had need be kind in it. I'll serve you about Dagenham or any thing else in my power, being your real friend and servant, J. Banks.
You never told me how you liked my observations on the papers you sent me.

note.value: 72. THE REV. JOSEPH COPE TO JOSEPH BANKS I.

text.p: Kirkby on Been, 11 November 1718. I give your worship my humble and hearty thanks for your kind letter you sent me the other day, which I take for a true kindness, and if I had bin able I would have answered it the next day. Mr. Gelsthorpe hath bin with me the other day, and I gave him full satisfaction upon all accounts wherein I was concerned with his lords and masters, to whom he promised me to write to let them know everything how it was. As for the great wast mentioned in the wood, I doe not know that I had the least stick of it to my own use, neither root nor branch; and if you doe not already know I could easily inform you if I saw you. The wood was employed at the mill, and two gartrees of mine I bought and payed for, and ten pounds in dale boards, and another tree that cost me five pounds for a fulling mill stock, besides abundance of iron work and nails, and hundreds of days for workman's wages, whom I had for 6 pence a day and some meat; and you discharged me for working any longer for a good space of time; and afterwards when you was pleased they should work again I was forced to give them 12 pence, 18 pence a day, and two shillings and more; besides the fulling mill cost me above 3 score pounds building, and it and the tenters and hot press and plate and the mill tools were sold for little or nothing. So if I can get nothing of Gelsthorpe I shall loose 500 pounds by the mill, and I have bin as hardly and harshly dealt (with) all as I had bin the greatest knave upon earth; and you have discharged some tenants for paying me any tithes, which I can make it appear to you that you are in the wrong of it; and whenever I dye my Lord Chancellor will put in a minister tithes and a great deal more, which I can and will make it plain see you. In the meantime I pray God to bless you and all yours and prosperity, which is all at present from your weak and very humble ilst, Jose: Cope. I have ngs to inform you of but I am not able at present.

note.value: 74. JOSEPH BANKS II TO JOSEPH BANKS I.

text.p: Revesby, 16 January 1720. I communicated yours to W. B. and considered matters with him before I sent for Mr. James, and what's underwritt is the best terms I can get him too, so W. B. is as capable to follow your directions as if I myself was here, and Mr. James desires an answer by the return of the post.
He will take all Tupholm's farm att 70£ a year, and only insist of having the house and particularly the roof repaired well att your charge, which will be no great matter when your here to direct it.

He will keep the high field lands, and his father's 18£ a year att the present rent, and the upper part of Tom Clerk's farm att 50£. So what he will part from is his 13£ a year, late Dr. Loves, Clamp Close and Abbey ground, which he pays dear enough for, and his homestead with all below it att 30£ a year.

But as to his Rowborrows he's unwilling to part from it on any terms, and says he pays you at least 12£ a year for it, if you consider what his plowd marlins abated the rent of the whole, and that Tom Clark was charged 11£ for it in Lord Barkshire's time.

This is the state of this matter, and now you'll expect me to say something. My opinion is that as you have high lands enough to spare about St. Sides, you'll not be in such need of Rowborough as you seem to fear; but then I can't flatter you with hopes of any great matters of rise from his low farm, tho doubt not but it will advance perhaps 6 or 7£ a year, which I know is nothing of what you'll expect may be raised in his farm, but you must consider, he keeps near 2 3rds of his old farm att least att an equal proportion of rent to the rest.

W. B. perfectly understands what I write to you, and has a copy of it, and will pursue your directions, which he begs may be very plain, for he is not scholar enough to understand so great a calculation by way of value per acres etc. as the nature of so great a farm requires, and I shall not be here to advise him.

Of Thursday last we had our wood sale, where we had but a very small appearance to what I have seen, nor could I in any manner answer your expectation in selling the wood (which I feared before you left Revesby), so after about 5 hours talking with the company, we parted without selling them any but 5 or 6 pieces in Sherwood att about 18d. per pol which tho it be as good as the sale in general is, nay better by 3d. per pol, is, I doubt, far short of your expectation.

The country generally complain they lost by the wood they bought of me the last year, and that there are great quantities now before hand, and likewise that there was so dry a season this last summer, that great quantities of fen fuel were got, which hinders the sale of kidwood.

And now give me leave to tell you that I never viewed wood more exactly then I did these two sales (having so fatigued myself 2 days together as I will not tell you), and truly find Fulsby sale much worse then I ever saw it, so that I fear 10£ an acre will stretch it when ever it is sold, and 12£ an acre for Sherwood the like. I'm sorry I can't give you a more satisfactory account of this affair, and assure you I've not been wanting in what in my power; so please to consider and order what you think convenient on the whole, and if I can be serviceable to you, shall be very ready to make another journey over.
I can't get the bricklayer near me, but have given Wm such instructions that he can't mistake me about his drawing.

And as to the brickmakers I agree with you that they are a pack of rogues, tho both Dickinson and the Bilingay men promise me to go on with there work, but the Bilingay men shut have some monies when they have turned the clay, else can't subsist. I will let Holden's farm before I go away if he gives me not good security.
I've given full directions about the planting, and likewise to buy you oats. I fancy they will scarce be cheaper then they are now.
I've made it my business to talk with all your tenants and neighbours about plowing your closes, but find 'em all engaged in there own affairs for the spring, so that I fear Wm will be pushed.
I've been with old Smith and several fen men, but find thatch so dear, it is not proper to lay in a quantity.

I this day finished receiving rents. The total of rents and arrears amounts to £231 13s. 0d. The copy of my receipts encloses a copy of your rental directed by Wm. The tenants that are now behind say they can't possibly pay before 18 or 20th of March. I've received the sum above exclusive of the taxes, so you may reckon on above 30£ more received. Tho even then it will be but a poor business to what you expected. I will take care for your bacon.

I have bottled your 2 hogsheads of Bawtry beer, it run seven dozen of the large quarts and 9 pints. I expected some more pints, but the vessel was reasonably full when spiled. Its good beer, but att present very flatt.
I hear Mr. Stevens can return your monies, tho in these parts I could not get any, so have order Wm to go of Monday morning with the monies to him and hope you'll get it soon.

My most humble duty and affectionate love attend you, my dear mother, brother and sister. I heartily wish you all health and happiness. I am, dear Sir, your most dutiful son and obedient servant, J. Banks.

P.S. Poor Lattice has been very ill since I came hither, but Mrs. Tupholme sends me word she is better. Here is the greatest mortality that ever was known in these parts, but much greater in the fens. Leak and Leverton have buried half of there inhabitants, as reported.
I thank you for your news of prosecution to be within a year, etc.

The 2 Agers of Moorby are about selling there farms to Mr. Hamerton off Horncastle, att 195£ each, but have a month's time to redeem them, and will let me have them att 200£ each, tho att the most improved value they are but let att £9 each, the landlord pays land tax, which is as dear as an egg a penny. So if you've a mind to purchase one or both of 'em please to signify it in a post or 2 to me for fear the time of redeeming be lost. Mr. Hamerton buys whatever he can in Moorby or Enderby, tho never so dear. He know nothing that I am on the scent of it.

note.value: 75. JOSEPH BANKS II TO JOSEPH BANKS I.

text.p: Revesby, 19 February 1720. Yours of the 9th instant I received in course, and am very sorry poor Jo still continues ill. Thank God my wife was better when I left her, and Lattice is got very well, as I hope this will find you, and all my good friends in Boswell Court, on whom my affectionate duty and love attend.

Considering the posture of your affairs here I judged it requisite for me to come over to see how all matters went on, and in the first place I took a view of Sir John Hales estate att Bollinbroke, which if it can be bought to your mind, will give you an entire principality in these parts, Sir John being chief lord of many neighbouring towns appurtenance to his manor of Bollinbrooke, which att this time they are endeavouring gradually to excuse. Likewise all the touls taken in all these parts are belonging to it, so that if you was possessed of it, I am persuaded you would do great things with it. I would have viewed every particular of the land but could not get it shown, the tenants being all sick or from home. They generally complain tic very dear, tho the neighbours say tic a handsome peniworth, and that there is one farm in the tenure of Mr. Hereby the attorney that will improve. If Jarvis Scroope be in Town he will manage this affair so as for Sir John to offer it you, but I fear he's left London so if I find him att Lincoln will get him to write forthwith to Sir John. The wood by Will Wests and another called Hall Hill near Earsby, much larger, belong to this estate.

I have bought George Agar's estate att Moorby cheaper then I expected, tho tic dear enough in reason: enclosed is the article.
The other brother will not sell for a deal more, and the division was perfectly equal. The lands are mortgaged to Mr. Hamerton of Horncastle, so he must be consulted when he will have his monies paid in, which I will do, and endeavour to get him stay till Lamas; if not, he must have it att Ladiday. On second thoughts it had much better be att Lamas, then you might draw the conveyance and see your title.

I have got a seemingly honest fellow and a good workman of a bricklayer from Spilsby. He has been 2 days att work with me here, and will come and finish the rest of Monday 3 weeks, against which time we will have lime burnt for him. I have given the fellow full instructions.
I have warned your rent day with some threats, and have got some returns, and will lay out for more. I've order 170£ to be paid you in 14 days or thereabouts.
Your tenant Smedley is dead, and I have seized of what he had, and wish it will pay you. It shall do as far as it can. I will leave orders with Wm how to proceed.

All the world stand amazed att S. S. Stock. I'm sorry for your misfortune as well as my own; dare say F. H. has got well by it. Fancy .... is as you write. I'm sorry you give yourself any trouble about him.

My servant directs you a copy of the wood sale, which I fear you'll not approve; however, assure you no more could have been made. I think it proper for W. B. to sell what remains standing as well as he can; am sure you'll lose by it if it either stands or you work it up. I wish you have sail for your kids and polls (before rotten) that you worked up last year. There has been so much of this sort of wood cut lately. Mr. Wright never sold such a sale or anything like it.
Sherwood I'm of opinion is sold dear enough. The three Not. men whom I met would not budge above 11£ per acre. The viewed our firths but can find no land fit for hops att all.
It is now time to order your brewing 2 or 3 hogsheads of ale or 7 of small beer, it would be the better to brew soon. They must set it in the outward seller. Direct Wm in that point.
Your brickmaking goes on very slowly. They Bilingay men are quite run off and Holden is very sick and fallen to the parish, tho Dickinson and he promise fair.

W. B. says you once offered him to let him Smedley's farm and build him a room. He desires me to acquaint you that if you be of that mind now, and will lay him the 2 closes now Flater's to it, and continue his salary to look after your woods, he will settle in this country and look no further. I have nothing farther to add but that I am your most dutiful son and obedient servant, J. Banks.

note.value: 76. WILLIAM BURBIDGE TO JOSEPH BANKS II.

text.p: Lincoln, 8th March 1721. Honoured Sir, John got. safe to Revesby on Saturday night and every thing very well, but the bay mares back is a little bruised. He went over to Donabys with her, but he was not at home, but William Banks promised to go over with her and send us word what Donaby said of her.
The bill of charges for his coming down.

Sir, we came here yesterday and found every thing very well. Both misses are very well but Miss Lattice heal is a little sore yet. Sir, this is Mary's bill for the twelve shilling. Mary Brinkley left when she came to Revesby. She cannot remember the day of the month when you had these things.
Sir, there is 21 quarters of oats come into the chamber but we have not measured them yet, but will send you an exact account next post.
Sir, there was one came here last week to summons you to be upon the grand jury. He spoke to Will but he doth not know the man's name that came.
The bill for the gin left Mary.

Sir, Mrs. Ann saith that all the things is lock that was in the work drawer so there is nothing to make Miss Lattices nor Miss Bettys caps on. Mrs. Heseltine saith that bibs and aprons is worn and not frocks now there in morning so if you please to give her leve she make some of that holland you send down. Miss wants some black stockings and gloves and we can get none here. No more at present from your most humble servant.
Wm. Burbidge.

note.value: 77. WILLIAM BURBIDGE TO JOSEPH BANKS II.

text.p:
15th March 1721. Honoured Sir, Mr. Royal will get the windows done as speedily as he can. Willaby came here to work on Monday last and began to take the window down in the passage,
but it is so rotten that it will do no good, so haith left it there and is mending the side of the house next the garden as you ordered.
Sir, he thinks it will be a great hazard to pull down that window in the passage to make a door there, for he saith the house is so cract it will be in great danger of falling.

Sir, Robert Brakenbury and the other men came here on Monday night last, but Mr. Brackenbury could not but in the trial until this morning about nine o'clock, but you have got it. It hardly held an argement it was so plain. Sir, Robert Brakenbury did not bring the note, so have not paid him, from your most humble servant, Wm. Burbidge.

note.value: 78. WILLIAM BURBIDGE TO JOSEPH BANKS II.

text.p: 18 March 1721. Honoured Sir, I spoke to Prigon to brue a hogshead and half of strong beer, but he said he could not promise me to come until today, so went down last night to know when he could come, but as he said he brewed all for Mrs. Sandby at the White hart and she had now almost 20 quarters to brew to go to Boston, so desired you to excuse him for it was impossible for to do it now. Sir, William is now brewing 6 strike for 3 hogsheads of small beer.
Please to see the bill of disburstments from March the 12th to the 18th 1720-21.

note.value: BILL OMITTED

text.p: Sir, the strong waters that is set down in the bill was for the old man that came for a witness that morning he was going he would have six pence in his pocket and his bottle of brandy or he would not go out of the house.
Sir, John desired me to let you know straw is very reasonable now and if you stay in Lincoln you would not have to serve you until new came again so if you think fit to buy a load or two more.

Sir, Miss Lattice and Miss Betty is very well and gives their duties. Nancy desires to know whether you will send some
cambric and holland for Misses mobs for you locked all the holand up.
The workman's names and days they have worked here this week.

note.value: LIST OMITTED

text.p: from your most humble servant, Wm. Burbidge.

note.value: 80. WILLIAM BURBIDGE TO JOSEPH BANKS II.

text.p: 1 April 1721. Mr. Potter hath not done the pails yet, but promises they shall be done and nailed up by the next Saturday without fail. Sir, there was no ordinary briks to be got, so Willaby spoke for a load of square ones such as the kitchen is paved with. He saith they are the cheapest for ware, so he on this day will pave it. Sir, Mrs. Haseledine hath hired two maids. Sir, the gardiner came here yesterday and saith the bay mares back is a great deal worse but when we came away John told me there was no danger but it would be well in two or three days.
The disburstments from March the 27th to April the 1, 1721.

note.value: LIST OMITTED

text.p: Sir, we have had a missfortain with which I thought fit to acquaint you with. The last night the mare Cate got loose and run a bit of wood under her shoulder, but I hope it will be well in a short time, from your most humble servant, Wm. Burbidge.

note.value: 81. WILLIAM BURBIDGE TO JOSEPH BANKS II.

text.p:
I beg pardon I did not write before now, but did not come out of Derbyshire till Saturday, and before I had got the letter write the post was gone out. Sir, in your last you write that you would have Mr. Dickinson to take the close of your hands. John protests that he never hard word of it until your letter came. Sir, Mr. Dickinson doth not desire any thing for the dressing the close but
saith it was not in his bargain, but will not be .... to the cleaning the close and repairing the hedges.

Sir, the bay mare's back was not so very ill when we came away from Revesby. I wrote word as John told me, and so did Donaby's man say it would soon be well. Sir, I could say no more then they told me. To be sure you had more judgment in those matters then I or at least should have. I wrote to Revesby but have had no answer as yet. Thank God Cate mends very fast. Sir, I am sorry I should make such a mistake in the strong beer, but thought you would know what it meant.

Sir, Joseph Hodgkinson desired me to send you word that he had got the moneys ready, and hoped you would be there to receive it, for it would be hard for him to pay interest in boath places. Sir, Mr. Hodgkinson bid me send word how long since Susana Bunting's father died for I suppose the Hackleas lease was taken that year he died. She saith it was fourteen years the 7th day of this month. Sir, if you please to put in to me, for I think it will go sooner from you then from here if you please to give your self that trouble. Sir, I inquired about a man, but could hear of none, but Godfery Hodgkinson he would very fine come, and doth not doubt but he could please you. I told him his business was not only for shooting but must do several other things, but he said he did not doubt but he should please, and for wage he would not differ if he had nothing, so did not bid him anything until I had a letter from you. They are all very well in Derbyshire.
The disburstments from Monday the 3th of April to the 10th 1721.
Potter hath done the pales. The prowler is come and we have taken the old frame and but it to the new .... Honoured Sir, from your most humble servant, Wm. Burbidge.

note.value: 83. WILLIAM BURBIDGE TO JOSEPH BANKS II.

text.p: 1 May 1721. We have got a henn to sit the eggs when they come but must pay 2s. 6d. for her sitting. We went all up and down but could not get one under that price. Sir, Thomas Aspen hath one half of the glases and the other is on cucumbers for selves. Sir, the pantry is finished all but the cubard that you purpose to be done when you come down and the windows which the glass is not put in yet. The parlour harth is done and the door and garden door that goes into the yard. The pails are done but the door is not hung yet. The windows in the best room are done. I do not know of any thing else to do except you please to have the harth in the kitchen mended. Mary was saying you talked something of that when you was down. Sir, Miss Lattice face is mended. The old scarr is a great deal better than when you went, but the other is as ill as ever but no running.
Sir, there is very little of the baccon flitches cut of. John hath not been well so had a mind of a bit of baccon. I think there was about 1/2 a pound cut of.

note.value: LIST OMITTED

text.p: Sir, we here hare that my Mrs. is ill but hope it is not true but a great many comes to inquire how she doth.

Sir, Miss Lattice wants a hoop ever ill. This is so bad she hath she can scarce ware it. Sir, you desired to know what clerks was at Horcastle. There was Mr. Boughwright's clark and Mr. Grantham's. Mr. Boughwright's clark had the share that I had, but the other had £5. 4s. There was a 11 in all. My share at Gainsborough and here was £4. 18s. Honoured Sir, from your most humble servant, Wm. Burbidge.
Mrs. Jinkinson is something better than she was but very wake.

note.value: 86. WILLIAM BURBIDGE TO JOSEPH BANKS II.

text.p: Lincoln, 18 June 1721 . The garden sith is so bad it is impossible to use it in mowing the close. Sir, I am sure you had better hire a man to mow the close then set Will to it he knows nothing of mowing he would leave more grass uncut then would pay a man his hire. If you would please to ask John he can satisfy you. Sir, I believe the close at Bracebridge will want mowing in a short time if the whether would take up. Sir, it was not Prigon that brewed strong beer, it was John Cumpton. I paid him as soon as he brewed the brewing. If you please to look over the letter I sent about the 29 of March you will find it therein. Sir, both misses are very well, from your most humble servant Wm Burbidge.

note.value: 92. JOSEPH BANKS II TO JOSEPH BANKS I.

text.p: Revesby, 12 February 1722. My wife and self were very much surprised last night with the melancholy news of my dear mother's death, and most heartily condole with you thereupon. I've this day sent a servant to Lincoln to fetch me your letters both of yesterday and to-morrow, and if I receive them soon enough will give you an answer by this post, if not of Wedensday.

My wife and I have considered of your desiring me in Town, and since this fatal accident has happened, it must remove all suspicion about my coming to Town; so if you please to give leave both my wife and self will wait of you the week after the
next, for fancy our being together after such a misfortune will be agreeable to us all. If you think our coming proper we shall bring no maid servant and only one man, and so keep house till we be fitted with mourning etc., and my wife will endeavour to get a maid in Town, for we have given Nany Brinkley notice to leave us. If on the contrary you do not approve this our design, I beg Mr. Harry will order our mourning, and that it may be sent us hither by the Louth carrier as soon as ready, and we will stay here till we get them. I beg pardon for the freedom above, but shall be perfectly pleased to do just as you please. We do not propose to bring any horses if we come.

Wm. Banks having let all the lands has nothing material to write so omits this week. My wife joins with me in humble duty to you, with affectionate love to our brother and sister, heartily wishing you all health, and am, dear Sir, your most dutiful son and obedient humble servant, J. Banks.

note.value: 94. JOSEPH BANKS II TO JOSEPH BANKS I.

text.p: Revesby, 8 February 1724. Enclosed comes your measures about the rooms, and also an affidavit which Mr. Robertson tells me you know the affair and desires you will assist him, for that Mr. Manby very much oppresses the country by this chicanery.
Doubleday's men go on very well, and we can't possibly get the ditch under 2s. an acre so big as you would have it, and it will be dear earnd. It's all hard chalk.

We have had a very poor receipt. In all with what oddments William received before I came £90. 12. 4 and near fifty of it disbursed. You shall have the particulars as soon as I get home to make them out. The cry of want of moneys is grevious, and tho perhaps you'll think much that I get no more, I have the worst of it in hearing their complaints. I have taken what precaution I can that you loose nothing in the end, and have sharpened them up as much as I can, and will be with 'em again the latter end of the month. I have settled and received the rents of most of the leaders, but I assure you they grumble heavily, and whether I can get 'em to lead any more I know not. However, they'll not meddle att the present tho I've offered to pay them as they bring each load in.

The parson Mr. Alexander has been with me again. I like him very well. He says now he does shoot, but durst not since he came of this side. He will be shortly in London, where I've ordered him wait of you. He seems to me very likely to fit you.
I have had a chapman or 2 for half or a 4th of the old stack, but no body yett will buy the outsides tho I've offered to cut 2 yards deep. They offer us six pound for half the stack and that's all.

But methinks if it was mine I would get another pair of bullocks and give them all the worst of the outside and the wood close hay (which no body has yett offered to buy) and so lead all home myself. If you come soon you'll want a good .... for yourself.

The leading all the stulps rails and pales take 2 horses every other day and sometimes every day, and have done as long
as they can without hay, that I believe what I advise will be the only way.

There's no such thing as a draught's going to Boston, as I have wrote twice to Mr. Palfreman, tho I never could get an answer from him, and its but reasonable. He brings 'em down to the fenn side down the dichch to Cow Bridge. Since he has kept 'em so long pray write sharply to him to that purpose.
Your plaster is not comed tho the boats are returned. The Trent was so much out that they could not find the plaster and fish it up.

I can't as yett get a brickmaker under 5s. per 1000, 5 score to the hundred, to take the clay as it is, but am trying what I can do, but shall conclude with him in a week if I can't get it under or be not country ordered by you. Pray what quantity do you depend on from J. Rogers?
What can be done with P. James is done both by Mr. Short and William, but he will stay att home. The other affair about Newcomen I am doing what I can in.
I hear Whelpdale's giving out great words that he's come here again, but I've order William, no parson but Alexander comes into the church, who I have ordered at present to attend the cure.
Your brewing and bottling I will take care of. I have now given the vessels out to be mended and we will go briskly on when I come over the end of this month.
We have sold about 14 or 15 pieces of the wood unsold, so if he get 6 or 8 more in about 10 days sold we will have another sale. I am, dear Sir, your most dutiful son and obedient servant, J. Banks.
I hear matters in the election go on very well of this side all over, but am now in the dark for the other parts.

note.value: 95. JOHN BLACKBONE TO JOSEPH BANKS I.

text.p:
Boston, 9 February 1725. I received yours and return you thanks for your favour towards me in speaking to Mr. Viner. As to Nordike bridge, I have the stone ready to begin it as soon as your honour comes down, for I think the weather is not proper to begin it at present. In taking down the old church and rebuilding it your honour desires to know the lowest price what I will take by the square yard or rood 7 yards long and a yard high to the rood, the lowest I can doe it for is 6s. six shilling per yard, you finding stone brick and lime and all other materials. As to the windows and doors I have included them, for we find more trouble in those things then in solid work. If your honour don't like the
above proposal I am willing to do the job for you by the day as you and I can agree, and will make the stone hold out as far as I can, but am afraid there will be a want. I am, your honor's most obedient humble servant, John Blackbone.

note.value: 100. THE REV. JOSEPH BANKS, RECTOR OF HOOTON ROBERTS, AND SON OF THE REV. ROBERT BANKS OF HULL, TO HIS UNCLE JOSEPH BANKS I, AT REVESBY ("TURN AT STILTON ").

text.p: Hooton Roberts, 30 August 1726. I had sooner sent you my hearty congratulations, as I now do, for your recovery from your late indisposition, but that I have been in daily expectation, for a considerable time, of giving you an account of my wife getting into the straw; and though she has far outgone her reckoning, yet I thank God is at last safely delivered of a boy, and both in a hopeful way of doing well.

Here is likely to be a great contest betwixt the two candidates who offer themselves for this county, viz.: Sir John Kay and Mr. Turner. Sir Thomas Wentworth (from whom and his late worthy father I received many favours) has sent to me to desire my vote for the latter, whom I would willingly oblige if you think it proper; besides I hear His Grace the Archbishop of York favours that interest, so that it may be a step, some time or other, towards preferment, but I shall act entirely in favour of your determination.

Mrs. Rayner, my mother's sister, and old Mr. Steer are lately dead. My mother seems very hearty and presents you with her most affectionate humble service, and my spouse with your godson join with me in humble duty, and in hearty love and service to good cousins as you see them, and I am, honoured Sir, your most dutiful nephew and obliged humble servant, Jo: Banks.

My little house fills apace, so that I am about sending out my eldest son to school, as soon as I hear of a good master and cheap board. The master in this town teaches no further than grammar, besides writing, and the first 4 rules in arithmetic, which my boy has gone throe: it will straiten me pretty much, but I am resolved to do what I can for him, being a sprightly youth, and of a promising genius. My new enclosure cleared about £16 this year, thanks to you for your kind assistance towards it.

note.value: 101. JOSEPH BANKS I TO THE REV. JOSEPH BANKS (DRAFT).

text.p: Lincoln, 10 September 1726. As to my godson, would have you send him to some northern school. My chaplain tells me of 2, where boys are kept close to their books, as well as educated much cheaper. He assures me the best boys pay but £5 a year board, and the schools are free, both in Westmorland, one called Hawkshead and the other , where the boys of London, Carlisle and many other great men were educated. If you'll carry him to one of these schools, into which gaiety pleasures etc seems not yet crept, as into most schools, I will at every years end while he stays there, give you five pounds towards his education, till you get better preferment. J. Banks.

note.value: 109. THE REV. MATTHEW ALEXANDER TO JOSEPH BANKS II.

text.p: Tattershall, 21 October 1728. On Saturday I received your most kind obliging letter, with three enclosed, which justly claims my best and most humble thanks; and notwithstanding your most industrious endeavours (by reason of your great distance) were attended with no better success, I am under the same obligations of gratitude for them and shall always be glad of opportunity to express it.

Mr. Shepherd, the Rector of Mareham, was at our house eight or nine days. He appears a gentleman of good temper, civility and ingenuity. He offered me the cure upon the same terms I had it. He intends to be down again in the spring and stay summer here and winter in Westmoreland, where he was born. Mr. Carr of Hemingby has got Sturton through the High Sheriff's interest to the Duke of Ancestor.
The country about us is generally in a very good state of health. I hear there's an epidemical fever about Surfleet and Pinchbeck that carries off abundance.
Dr. King of Stamford died of a raging fever, raving mad, a week ago.
Mr. Brown will give account of the drains from Wm. Banks' mouth, I know there's opposition about the payment of the money, and I believe all occasioned by Mr. Kelham.

It is agreed on all hands here that Moorby is void ipso facto by Mr. Sympson's taking another living out of distance. Mr. Shepherd promised to enquire of the Bishop of Carlisle about it and use his interest for me and recomend me to him; I humbly beg you'll please to write, in my favour, to the Bishop. Further, since Mr. Shepherd went away, Mr. Allen (whom you know) an utter enemy of Sympson's, publicly declared, at the Visitation, as soon as it was lapsed he would take out the seals, by which means the good Bishop will loose his turn of presentation.

I was at Revesby yesterday morning, when all was well. Miss has been and continues in perfect health, ever since you left us, and presents her duty to your self and Momma, which with my most hearty thanks and service to your self and Lady for all favours, concludes me, honoured Sir, your most obliged humble servant and chaplain, Mat. Alexander.
P.S. The Bishop of Lincoln's son is made Chancellor of the Church of Lincoln, since married to Dr. Ball's daughter. The Bishop of Peterborough's son is presented to Burton Coggles.

note.value: 120. THE REV. MATTHEW ALEXANDER TO JOSEPH BANKS II.

text.p: Tattershall, 16 December 1728. I writ you my hearty thanks to Bristol for your kind endeavours about Mareham and Sturton, which I hope you received: and here, under the deepest sense of gratitude, I repeat them. At the same time, I intimated, that Moorby was void, as all about us believe, and begged your address to the Bishop of Carlisle in my favour. But not hearing anything since you came to Town, take leave to name it again.

About 10 days ago I received a subpoena to give evidence in a trial at Boston, betwixt Thomas Rastal and John Proudlove, concerning a years rent of Scarshill close. After a long hearing the jury found it for the former. Doubleday and Bee were evidences for Proudlove, two very great rogues and dangerous people to live near. I'm glad they are so far distant from us. Had they known what would have done I'm confident they would have sworn it. The Court did not think proper to administer an oath to Doubleday's wife, who was there, ready to swallow it.

It has pleased God to visit this corner with an epidemic and very mortal distemper. Mr. Wright says it is a pleuretic fever, which carries off abundance in 3 or 4 days illness; but I think in and about Revesby the symptoms seem to me somewhat different from those I have visited at Tatsal and Cunsby &c., their throats being generally sorr and their heads swelled to an uncommon size. I buried seven last week at Mareham and Revesby, and am going this afternoon to bury two at the latter place, one of which is Frank Keel (whose wife I buried Sunday seven-night), and I heard last night that his settlement admits of a dispute betwixt Revesby and East Kirkby. Mr. Oliver Comptroller of the Customs in Boston is dead.

I congratulate you on your safe arrival in Town from Bath, and I pray God preserve your health, your lady's and your hopeful issues, and heartily send you the compliments of the approaching season, and am your most obliged obedient humble servant, Mat. Alexander.

TEI.text:
Tattershall, 10 February 1729. I am sorry for your engagement with the cunning Quaker. I was not at Revesby when he came there upon his journey to Well. But on a Sunday, upon our coming from Church, in the afternoon, I remember very well his being in the kitchen, after his return from Mr. Bateman's; that he went into the coachhouse with you; that you were about an agreement with him for a chariot (for I was then in the court-yard); and after that he was with you and Mrs. Banks in the parlour; and at his return into the kitchen I was there again, and said to him "Now John, have you agreed?" He answered "Yes, I think so, but their minds are changed, they'll now have a chariot". I replied "You may afford to work cheaper for Mr. Banks than another, considering I dare say, you got by the funeral, for" said I, " I took off the mourning upon the pulpit and d was not worth so much money, by a third more, you charged in your proposals for undertaking it." That, he said, he could not help att such times; they were at a great expense. But this he left to his master and .... see, he would please him. This is what betwixt us and all that occurs to my memory at present. It was a little before you left the country, do not know, but the Sunday or Sunday seven-night before.
As to my own affairs, I give you my humble thanks for preventing the present process. I have the greatest rogue upon the earth to deal with; his demands, till now, were £5. 13. 0 and he ordered an attorney to sue me for that sum, as appears by the attorney's letters now in my hand. I communicated the affair to your father, who ordered me to answer them in such manner as should induce
them to believe I was protected (though he never premised me any such thing) in order to bring him to an account. He is in goal and has been some years, and owes me considerably more than I him. But he expects to be freed by the approaching Act, and sues every body who owes him any thing and will come to no account. Now, in order to hold me to bail, he has sworn to £10.6.0, which I never heard on before; he drew several bills upon me for the aforesaid sum, which I returned, and several of this neighbourhood were with him this summer, and he cl for £5 or thereabouts. I never borrowed of him in my life. It is well known to the whole country that he was always in my debt from our first acquaintance. I have a bill in my father's hand for 6 or 7 for goods bought of me. I have a note here for 2-8 I paid for sister to whom he is executor, besides due for her board and a horse he himself had
multis aliis .
For all this, I find, I must be answerable to him for some part of this debt, and I doubt lose all my own money.
Since I writ the other sides I came to Horncastle and took Mr. Hammerton's advice in the affair, showed my bill and letters from his other attorney and told him the case; who tells me, though I am sure he cannot prove, what he has swear, that it will be a great expense, and since hoe's worth nothing and in goal and will come to no account, and I likely to be a great sufferer, yet still my way is to agree if possible with him, for common bail and then special bail, he says, will at first cost £5.
My father has been about an agreement with him some time, and he offered at last to take the £5.13.0. But my father knowing I was to be so great a loser would not comply, and now the villain taken these measures. I have writ to ning the affair and enclosed it, which I beg you'll forward, and hope it be not inconsistent with your Honour. You'll protect me from the and villainy of such a fellow, till something can be done.
I spoke to Jo. Stanley and Tom Hackford about grey plover, who tell me they have not seen one this year, but if they catch or hear of any taken, promise to let me know. I'll lay my endeavours out elsewhere in the fen.
I am very sorry my letters should prevent your coming to Revesby, but I hope it is better than if you had in person been surprised with the great mortality, which is not only our fate at Revesby and Mareham, but at several would towns, where whole families are carried off, and I hear this morning many die at and about Boston.
I broke my gun six weeks ago, but hope to have it this week, and will do what I can that you may taste more of your own game.
I humbly leave it to you to return an answer to Mr. Beck's agent, and beg Mr. Brown will acquaint me what he says,
and am, honoured Sir, your most servant and chaplain, Mat. Alexander.
Please to frank the enclosed to Mr. Shep .

note.value: 141. W(ILLIAM) GYLBY TO JOSEPH BANKS II.

text.p: 15 December 1729. I had the favour of yours, and as to the securities you propose (to which you desire an immediate answer) either of them seem to me to be very sufficient, and so I shall say if Mrs. Washington refers it to me. As to the value of the first security no objection can be made to it, but being a stranger to the nature of it, I can't judge of the title. But the second can admit of no exception (I think) either in respect of value or title, especially since £1000 of the purchase money will be paid (as I suppose) to Dr Greathead in discharge of his mortgage. You'll find me in Town when you come up. I am, Sir, your very humble servant, W. Gylby.

note.value: 154. ALICE NELSON TO JOSEPH BANKS II.

text.p:
21 March 1730. Worthy Sir, I have been in so great trouble for the dearth of dear Jack Norton mead me incapebell of doing myself the honour of writing: and hope you will pardon the liberty I take, and beg you will be so kind to let me have the money in your hand which will be great charity, I having given him what money I could spare ever since your father dearth, his coming in being but small. I had great hopes of his industery when he had been out of his time and believe hee would have mead a name. For all hee sofered a great deall and offed called out upon good Mr. Banks and send hee would help him out of all his troubles, this is the
last and only thing I shall trouble you with, and hope, good Sir, you will pit my great affliction and I hope God will bless you and your virtues lady and children with health and long liffe, which is the constant prayers of, worthy Sir, your most obliged humble servant, A. Nelson.
I am att the Judg's lodgings in Nottingham.

note.value: 159. THE REV. JOSEPH BANKS TO JOSEPH BANKS II.

text.p: Hooton Roberts, 19 April 1730. I'm favoured with your kind letter, and return my most humble and hearty thanks for the trouble you have been at on my accounts. The living of Edlington is not yet disposed of, and though Brother Steer gave me hopes of succeeding if in Mr. Battys gift, as I presume it is, yet I hear (under the rose) that he calls it his perquisite, and has offered it to several upon such terms as have thought fit to reject his proposals; and I am sure I think it much better to do so, than not come fairly by it.

My spouse was safely delivered on Thursday last of a girl, and though she is very weak yet, I bless God, both in a hopeful way of doing well. My good Mother is something better, she and my wife join in affectionate humble service to your self and lady, and I am, good Sir, your very much obliged and thankful humble servant, Jo: Banks.

note.value: 166. ROBERT BANKS OF BAWTRY TO JOSEPH BANKS II.

text.p: Bawtry, .... 1730. I was favoured with yours, and have made the best inquiry I can about Peter Vampley, late of Hatfield but now of Gaton in the Marsh near Louth, which is as follows: - That he is a small farmer, lived 4 years servant with one Peter Lelew in our Levels, has one child by a former wife, and is lately married to a 2d, and as far as I can learn is not capable of stocking your ffarm without he has got considerably by his 2d wife, which I cannot learn, but it may be enquired of at Gayton. I was in hopes of seeing you in Town ere this, but things have fallen out so crossly that I could not, and I fear you will be gone out of Town before I come up in June. My very humble service attends you, good cozen, and all yours, and I am, dear Sir, your most obliged humble servant, To: Banks.

note.value: 173. WILLIAM BURBIDGE TO JOSEPH BANKS II, IN QUEEN'S SQUARE, LONDON.

text.p:
Revesby, 25 January 1731. Wednesday last I got back from Nottinghamshire: and to my great surprise found the house with the 12 acre Granthams and two other closes let. You
promised me in Mr. Sponsor's garden nothing should be meddeled with till you or some other by your order had vewd and inspected in it to see if it was to dare &c, and if so your abate rent, but nothing of that promise was thought on after, only to the contrary a letter was sent immediately to provide a tenant, neither was I admitted to forgo any but hold all or none, a trip designed as I suppose to undo me, but as you are so kind (to me who thought my self always happy if I could do any one thing even to the hazard of my life to please you) hope you will give me leave to make the best of the hay. I do not rate it cost me a great deal of money getting, and if I must leave it for the next scrub twill be very hard service done to your most humble servant, Wm. Burbidge.
On Tuesday the 12th instant your greyhounds worried me two more of my ewes big with lamb, the very best I have.

note.value: 180. ALICE NELSON TO JOSEPH BANKS II.

text.p:
11 April 1731. I had wrote to return you my humble thanks before now had I not been very ill. I sent a man and horse on purpose with yours enclosed to Mr Wright who was very hard with me. He would not bate won peney in the funeral charge tho he promised me he would bear the haleff if not all. I received a 11 pounds and one shilling but had the man and horse to pay out of that who was a week at Shifeld over Mr Wright before all things
was end. Sir, hear is a paper of Packs that was wrote when he was with you att Nottingham. If you pleas to give me live I will send it to you. I am, worthy Sir, your most obliged humble servant, A. Nelson.

note.value: 181. THE REV. MATTHEW ALEXANDER TO JOSEPH BANKS II.

text.p: Tattershall, 29 April 1731. I hope you received mine from Stilton, wherein I acquainted you with Sir John Shaw's caveat against my institution to Ewerby and my disappointment at Bugden: I now take leave to tell you that in my return yesterday I called at Ewerby, and find a good house, the situation pleasant and the living worth about 55 or 60£ per annum , and that I made an enquiry about Sir John's right of presentation. The neighbours say that the steward (one Taylor, now steward to the Lady Middleton at Stapleford near Newark) was wont to tell them that Sir John had a right by the marriage of the granddaughter of Sir Richard Rothwel, Barrt, who presented the last Incumbent. But now they say, though Sir Richard did present the last Incumbent, Mr Silvester Leech, it appeared that Sir Richard had no such right, and that Mr. Leech had been deprived of it, though he was instituted and inducted, had he not made interest to the then Lord Chancellor and taken out the Broad Seal. And he himself said it was in the gift of the Crown.

This is the best information I could get, and thought proper to lay it before you, and the Bishop too, the first post, for I was never under such apprehensions and dread of disappointment in my life. I would not give it out at Urby that I heard or knew of a caveat, lest it should make some of the clergy thereabouts that have apply'ed to Sir John more solicitous. I am, honoured Sir, your most obliged obedient humle servant, Mat. Alexander.

I may add that Mr Dobbs had been at Tattsal since I went abroad, and I find by some that keep him company that he imagines Tattsal will fall to young Shepherd at last, for want of better solicitations, for it is not disposed of.

note.value: 183. ALICE NELSON TO JOSEPH BANKS II.

text.p: The "gudg's lodging" Nottingham, 1 May 1731. I return my humbly thank for all favours and am bound to pray for your health and long life.

I have hear sent this paper off dear Jack good intentions towards me, and since God was pleased to take him to himselef before I had any comfort of him beg and desire, good Sir, you will be so charitebell to let me have the reminder of this bond of what was spent at Shiffeld since you was so good to give it once, and confess it woes your one goodness and not that I could have obliged you to the least for him. And now cannot help telling you Sir I have several times deigned having the hounderd a year settled upon me and mien if I would have been in Mrs Lees stead, that is house keeper to your father, but reather chose to get my bread by the sweet of my brow, knoweing it was against the laws of God and man, and to make this poor unfortnent youth easey with what you was pleased to give him left my selef viii lowe. I hope your great goodness will consider my loss in his absence. I am, worthy Sir, your ever obliged humble servant, A. Nelson.

note.value: 196. THE REV. JOSEPH BANKS TO JOSEPH BANKS II.

text.p: Hooton Roberts, 10 September 1732. I received the favour of your most obliging letter, and am sorry to hear that my son does not so much consider his own interest, as heartily to apply himself to writing and accounts at leisure hours; which shall be the first and surest step towards his preferment. He shall have my hearty resentment, and hope you'll be so good as to impute it to his years. As to his breaking out, it may perhaps be occasioned by change of air and diet, for I do assure you, he has had no illness of any kind that I remember (excepting the ague when very young) since he was born. I hope bleeding, if the apothecary thinks it proper, and some gentle physic will set him right again. We have a distemper in these parts which shows itself in various manners, sometimes like unto a rash, upon others like chicken pocks, on others like the itch, all which bleeding cream of tartar, or manna and Epsom salts cured. It is a pleasure and great comfort to me to hear that my child is a good boy, and return my most humble and hearty thanks for your great care of him, and hope God will reward you and yours for it. My spouse who, I bless God, is now very well, joins in humble service to your self, lady and cousins, with, honoured Sir, your very affectionate kinsman and most obliged humble servant, J. Banks.

note.value: 199. CATHERINE BANKS TO HER HUSBAND JOSEPH BANKS II.

text.p: 21 October 1732.

I received yours last post with the robe in it, but by the letter doe not find you expected the money tho they went for it. The nurse is come out of Hertfordshire tho I fear to little purpose, for the child was taken with fits last Thursday. I have Doctor Broxham only, believing none of them can doe it any service; so beg that you will not be surprised if you hear of an alteration. Nothing has been wanting that could be thought of, as blisters etc. I am very well, but cannot help saying in a great concern for the poor dear little creature; and hope to see you very soon, tho I beg of you not to hurry your self in any kind. Poor good Mrs Towler greves so much I wish she be able to go,
tho she has nothing to answer for; but pure ill fortune attends her. I am, dear Mr Banks, your most affectionate, C. Banks.

8 a clock. Doctor Broxham just tells me he has no hopes of the child; the nurss's thinks it cannot get this night over. If you would have it buried at Revesby send a servant up to me directly. If I hear nothing from you and we should have the expected change I imagine you would have it buried here in Town; and I think the privater the better.

note.value: 209. ROBERT BANKS OF BAWTRY TO JOSEPH BANKS II, IN ST. JAMES SQUARE.

text.p: 17 March 1733.

There is nothing but the necessity of my affairs could oblige me to give you this trouble, but as my estate is already in your hands, I cannot by any means raise moneys that I must pay in Town, or be ruined, but by your assistance.

I do assure you I have enough to pay you, exclusive of the estate mortgaged, could I but get it in but at present that is impossible, therefore humbly entreat the favour of your assistance at this time, and upon the word of a Christian I will pay you back 500 £ in 6 months time. Was I to suffer all that is possible for a man to suffer, I would not propose this matter to you was I not sensible of your being entirely safe, and as being so, hope you will prevent the ruin and destruction that may fall upon a ffamily only for want of a seasonable relief, and where it can be to you no loss. I beg you will consider this matter and let me feel that ffriendship you always professed for me. Dear Sir, your most affectionate and faithful humble servant, To: Banks.

note.value: 210. JOSEPH BANKS II TO HIS WIFE CATHERINE, AT HER HOUSE IN ST. JAMES' SQUARE.

text.p: Bath, 30 March 1733. I am vastly obligd to you for your most engaging letter and assure you, no news so agreeable to me as thy health and welfare, and for thy present twill add very much to my pleasure. I am very glad to hear it rumbles about.

I dare say I need not assure dear Kitty that her plan of happiness is perfectly agreeable to mine and that I spend no time so agreeable as with her, and do not wonder that every body show thee respect and are desirous of thy company which is always productive of cheerful pleasure.

I fancy the waters will do me good tho att present they strike all sorts of paths out, sometimes in one place sometimes another, but Dr Oliver says all will end well, but wants me mightily to make a longer stay, nay to winter here, which I believe I shall some time do, when Kitty likes to come here, tho here is no hunting.

I thank thee of all thy chitt chatt and wish I could send thee any from hence, we have no gallantrys of any kind that I hear of, nor no hangeing or drowning. The young lady you mention is very shocking. As for the lady I believe her character has always been of the most profligate.
Iv a great deal of service for thee. All your acquaintance are very well. I think few very bad. Mr Sicker I fear is eddying. Kitt Neville very hearty.

I design God willing to be punctual to my time and assure my dearest life every day till then will seem an age. Excuse my not writing to the girls and Billy, writing being bad for the waters. Adieu, my dearest, and accept the best of the wishes of thy most faithful, J. Banks.
Saturday Even.

Since I wrote my letter received thy most obliging letter with the enclosed you mention. As to thy lying in I earnestly desire it may be wherever it will give thee the most satisfaction. I am infinitely obliged to thee for desiring to be near me. I am sure it will give me great pleasure, but rather than that shall stand in your way I will come up with thee to London. Therefore unless you are perfectly satisfied, make no resolution. As to the affair of .... we are now got rid of suspicion, I have a opinion for all the she's made about it than the thing itself. I've burnt thy letter as you command, and shall not mention it, but think Mr B. may ketch a tartar. Perhaps he may not be so much displeased at the parting as we imagine. I expect next some discoveries will be made of her. But I can't say I am afraid these perplexities as they have muddled me a good .... will end ill of my side which shall be sorry for. I am, dearest Kitty, thine faithfully, J. B.

Pray tell Lattice I thank her for her letter. She sent me a letter from Mrs Lee to Mrs Woodman which seems to be of the same
kind. Mrs Lee sent to Jo. Patison for her money in it, but Lattice does not explain the least word why she sends it. So if she has anything to say she should send me word. I suppose as Mrs Woodman was gone into service Mrs Lee wrote to Jo. Patison.

note.value: 212. ANN HALES TO MRS. CATHERINE BANKS.

text.p: 7 May 1733. I received both your last letters, but am working myself a head, which I hope to finish before I see you (not having money for a laced one) and a suit of cloths besides, which I shall be glad if you choose me a flowered .... at Mr Jenings. I would go to ten shillings a yard. I would have it either a white or brown ground, which you think is most in fashion; a green short apron and a girdle, not a siver one, but one of the knit girdles. I wish you could buy me a slight nightgown (not India for I hate them); a stripped ... I should like to buy any where you please to buy it, and I will give you the money at Revesby. I think about two ginuas for the nightgown will do, and send them both together; for red to make they will cost too much for me making in London. I have ordered you no money, for pay day is not till June. I owe Jenyns not a farthing and my credit is good, if you say it is for Mrs Ann Hales, because we all buy of him. I desire but just as much as will make the suit and nightgown. I think I shall be exceeding smart, sure I shall pick up a Pilkington or some such pretty fellow this sumer. I am just wild, child, to know what your father is hatching. I insist in your next you write me the first letter of her name or I will never forgive you, for I have a strong reason for that but don't tell him so, for I have plauged him and s'you know what to marry, which I fancy they will both together. I am sure they are carrying on something that is vastly clever. I shall with great sincereity wish them both joy. I hope they will make a better appearance than our Earl and his Countess, for she has got a second Heardson. I have a thousand things to tell you upon that subject when we meet, which I care not how soon. You will soon, I believe, have one of our Lincoln Ladies your neibour, upon the Wolds she will be seated. She is a pretty black woman and one you very much like, but you shall not know her name till I have the other Ladies. Miss Ball has discarded Mr Beck, Miss Molly Cunington has for certain refused my cousin Nevill. I am quite angy at our Ladies over rateing themselves. It spoil the market for the rest.
